analysis.one_liner: Stops drug companies from restricting how safety-net clinics and hospitals buy and dispense discounted 340B drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in September 2024 and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended in January 2025 without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The 340B program requires drug makers to sell medicines at steep discounts to safety-net hospitals, community health centers, and clinics that serve low-income patients. In recent years, some manufacturers have refused to ship those discounted drugs to contract pharmacies or imposed limits on such arrangements. This bill would write into law that manufacturers must honor the discounts regardless of how or where the drug is dispensed, bar them from attaching conditions, and let the government fine violators up to $2 million per day. It never got a committee hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients of community health centers, rural hospitals, HIV and cancer clinics, and other safety-net providers benefit: the bill guarantees they can keep getting discounted medicines through contract pharmacies, including specialty and mail-order pharmacies that are often the only source for expensive chronic-disease drugs. The safety-net providers themselves gain leverage and fines against manufacturers that try to cut them off.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients of safety-net clinics and hospitals

how_it_helps.text: It writes into the law that drug makers must offer their discounted 340B prices to safety-net providers no matter how or where the drug is dispensed, including through contract pharmacies — the community and mail-order pharmacies that many clinics and rural hospitals rely on.

It bars manufacturers from conditioning sales on things like refusing delivery to a contract pharmacy, limiting where drugs may be dispensed, or demanding claims data — with civil money penalties of up to $2,000,000 per day for knowing violations.

It gives the Secretary of Health and Human Services a rulemaking deadline and a complaint process so covered entities can actually enforce these rights, instead of litigating manufacturer restrictions case by case.

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers bear the cost: they would lose the ability to restrict 340B sales, face civil penalties of up to $2 million per day for knowingly violating the rules, and would have to comply with new regulations within 180 days. To the extent the program grows, manufacturers sell more drugs at mandated discounts, and some of that cost may be passed through to prices elsewhere in the system.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not require covered entities to pass 340B savings on to patients, and critics of contract pharmacy expansion argue that some large hospitals use the program's discounts to grow revenue rather than lower patients' out-of-pocket costs.
The penalty provisions depend on regulations the Health and Human Services Secretary would write within 180 days, leaving the strength of enforcement largely in the administration's hands.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients of safety-net providers, the benefits were real and the costs largely fall on drug makers, who would face fines up to $2 million per day for cutting off discounted deliveries. An honest caveat: contract pharmacy expansion has also been used by some large hospitals to widen 340B margins beyond community care, and the bill does not require savings to flow to patients, so some of the benefit could be absorbed by institutions rather than lowering patients' costs. Still, the core change—no more refusals to ship discounted drugs—directly protects access to medicines for low-income patients.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2024, sent to the Senate health committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Peter Welch introduced the bill on September 11, 2024, near the end of the 118th Congress.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — the standard first step, which sent it to the committee's queue rather than the floor.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers keep the ability to limit 340B discounted-drug shipments to contract pharmacies; safety-net patients gain nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers, who keep their current leverage

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave it its only sponsorship.

for.name: Senate HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the referred bill and took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat with one Democratic cosponsor and never reached a vote, so no party split on it was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would force manufacturers to keep shipping discounted drugs to contract pharmacies and forbid them from attaching conditions, backed by civil penalties of up to $2 million per day of violation. Manufacturers have sought these restrictions to curb the growing size of the 340B program.

Community, specialty, and mail-order pharmacies would gain legal protection for their 340B dispensing relationships with clinics and hospitals, since manufacturers could no longer refuse to ship or condition discounted drugs on those arrangements.

industries.industry: 340B covered entities (hospitals, community health centers, clinics)
industries.note: Safety-net providers would keep unrestricted access to discounted drugs through contract pharmacies, entrenching the 340B program's existing structure. That helps low-income patients served by these providers, though the bill leaves the entities free to decide how to use the savings.
